function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or any registry you prefer) whenever you push to `main`.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to your repo from here, but the commands below will get everything done locally and then push it back to GitHub.

---

## 1. Clone the repo (locally)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Create / update the following files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> - `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> - `npm ci` guarantees a clean install of exactly the versions in `package-lock.json`.  
> - The container listens on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a folder called `k8s` at the root of the repo and add two files inside it.

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace <YOUR_REGISTRY>
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # External port exposed by the service
    targetPort: 3000          # Port inside the pod
```

> **Tip** – If you’re deploying to a local cluster (e.g., Minikube), change `type: LoadBalancer` to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    # Optional: Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a kubeconfig secret)
    # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
    #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
    #   with:
    #     manifests: |
    #       ./k8s/deployment.yaml
    #       ./k8s/service.yaml
    #     images: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
    #     kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **What you need to set up in GitHub:**
> 1. **Secrets**  
>    - `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username.  
>    - `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password or an access token.  
>    - *(Optional)* `KUBECONFIG` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig if you want the workflow to deploy automatically.  
> 2. Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` in `k8s/deployment.yaml` with the same registry you’ll push to (e.g., `docker.io/<username>`).

---

## 3. Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4. Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, build the Docker image, and push it to your registry. If you enabled the optional Kubernetes deployment step, it will also apply the manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick Checklist

| Step | Command / Action | Done? |
|------|------------------|-------|
| Clone repo | `git clone ...` | ✅ |
| Create Dockerfile | `touch Dockerfile && edit` | ✅ |
| Create k8s folder & files | `mkdir k8s && touch deployment.yaml service.yaml` | ✅ |
| Create GitHub Actions workflow | `mkdir -p .github/workflows && touch ci.yml` | ✅ |
| Add files | `git add ...` | ✅ |
| Commit | `git commit -m "..."` | ✅ |
| Push | `git push origin main` | ✅ |
| Set GitHub secrets | In repo settings → Secrets | ❓ |

Feel free to tweak the replica count, service type, or Docker image tag as needed. Happy coding!
